To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) a growth rate decreasing (G) plasmid can coexist with a growth rate increasing (I) plasmid, but only if the transfer rate of the (G) plasmid is sufficiently low and its host fitness sufficiently high, and (ii) the presence of a G-plasmid can facilitate the invasion of a second I-plasmid, but the presence of the second I-plasmids will prevent the invasion of a third G-plasmid.

(1) a decreasing growth rate plasmid can be selected for in a bacterial population, and (2) the coexistence of plasmid types in a bacterial population is possible only if they follow a different survival strategy.

(1) the frequency of plsmid-bearers will tend to an asymptotically stable equilibrium if the population is under famine conditions, (2) the frequency of the plsmid-bearer will oscillate under feast conditions and (3) two incompatible plasmids can coexist if they follow a different survival strategy.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the conditions for coexistence of incompatible plas- mids in a population living under a fluctuating environment.
the evolution of plasmids in bacteria living in a fluctuating environment.

the evolution of a bacterial population living on a surface, which is covered with growth sites that get exhausted one by one, with a plasmid that is transferred from one bacterium to the other by conjugation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
plasmid coexistence is only possible under a very restricted set of conditions.
the coexistence of incompatible plasmds of the same incompatability group is impossible.
coexistence of two plasmids is possible, but only if the two plasmids have a different fitness.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the coexistence of two incompatible plasmids can only be expected in case of a feast-and-fame regime and that coexistence of three plasmaids is impossible.
the conditions for coexistence of plasmid types are rather stringent, and that the possibility for coexistence of two plasmids is much more likely than that of three plasmid types.
the coexistence of two incompatible plasmids is possible only when the two plasmids have different survival strategies.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the coexistence of plasmid strains in a population can be explained by a trade-off in their survival strategies.
plasmids with a lower fitness can invade and persist in a bacterial population.
coexistence of two plasmids is possible, provided that they follow different survival strategy.
